To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the level of fear induced by a message is a function of both the fear appeal and the individual; (2) the level of induced fear can be manipulated by the fear appeal and/or the individual; and (3) the level of the fear induced is a necessary condition for the persuasion effect.
(a) fear appeals are not more persuasive than other appeals, and (b) the optimal level of fear for persuasion is not the same for all individuals.
the optimal level of fear is the one that is appropriate for the target audience, and this level is not necessarily high fear.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the optimal fear level for persuasion is not an artifact of past research but the result of a theory, the "optimal level theory."
fear communications, like all others, can be effective or ineffective depending on a host of message and recipient variables.
fear appeals, when used appropriately in advertising, are a powerful persuasive tool, but the "optimal level" of fear is a myth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the optimal level of fear in a fear appeal depends on the nature of the message and the characteristics of the receiver.
fear appeals are not the only way to motivate people to take action and that the "optimal level" of fear for persuasion is a chimera.
